item.title: Why the under on runs looks like the smart baseball play when Pirates visit the Reds tonight
item.description: Paul Skenes and Hunter Greene face off as the Pittsburgh Pirates visit the Cincinnati Reds, with the under eight runs emerging as the smart play.
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday did not go as expected. I lost one game between the Giants and Padres as Robbie Ray spun a gem in what could be his last start for the squad. Sometimes you run into that, and all you can do is tip your cap to the other team. I'll suck it up and move on, and hopefully get some of that money back here today as we play the Pirates vs. the Reds.

The Pittsburgh Pirates seem to be in a similar cycle this season. They have one step forward and then one back. I suppose the good news is that they aren't going one step forward and two steps backward. They are exactly at .500 coming into today's game, sitting at 55-55 for the year. The final 52 games of the season will tell the story of whether this year is successful or not. Maybe that's harsh, because this still should be a step-forward season, and one they can use for momentum moving forward.

I've written about the importance of Pittsburgh being aggressive in using this window for them to make a consistently good team. If they don't, guys like today's starter, Paul Skenes, will start looking for ways off the team. Skenes is 9-9 for the season with a 3.65 ERA and a 1.06 WHIP. This is the worst season of his young career, but all of his numbers are 31st in the Majors or better. He has been worse on the road than at home, but not terrible. This has been a tough month for Skenes; he has allowed 17 earned runs in 27.2 innings of work. He has faced the Reds twice this season and allowed five earned runs in 10 innings of work.

The Cincinnati Reds took a step back this season after making the postseason. They started the season hot out of the gate. This team was 20-11 after April came to an end. Since then, they have gone 30-46. To start May, they lost eight consecutive games and went 4-13 to start the month. To start the second half of the season, they've gone 8-5. Perhaps the All-Star Break is what the team needed to make some adjustments.

There is more than enough time to make a run at the postseason, but they'll need to get some better performances from their pitching staff. The Reds do have some good pitchers, so the adjustments can be made. Today's starter, Hunter Greene, is one of the better young arms in the league, but he has struggled since he came into their rotation in early July. He has allowed 17 earned runs in 21.2 innings this season. In fairness to him, he has two quality starts and two disasters. Pirates hitters are batting .200 against him over 55 at-bats.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS

We have two aces on the mound, guys who have, or could someday, win Cy Young awards. However, neither has been exactly impressive when it comes to consistency. Skenes has struggled all month. Greene has allowed 14 earned runs in two starts, and three earned runs in his other two. Which version of these pitchers is showing up?

The Pirates haven't been playing great baseball lately, so it is really hard to back them, even with Skenes on the mound. The Reds have been terrible at home — 24-30. I think the smarter option here is to take the under eight runs. Both teams know the importance of this game, and both starters will know how crucial it is to give their team a chance. Neither team has great numbers against the opposing starter, so I'll back the under eight.

item.title: Investigators believe Iranian hackers are likely behind cyberattack on Minnesota water systems: report
item.description: More than 30 Minnesota water systems were hit by a coordinated cyberattack that officials say was likely orchestrated by Iranian hackers, a report said.
item.content:encoded:
U.S. investigators believe a cyberattack that targeted dozens of water systems in Minnesota this week likely was orchestrated by Iranian hackers, a report said.

Minnesota IT Services (MNIT) said the "coordinated cyberattack targeted operational technology at more than 30 Minnesota community water systems" on Sunday and Monday, but the Minnesota Department of Health is "not aware of any active requests from Minnesota cities to have their residents modify their drinking water usage."

U.S. and state officials and others familiar with the incident told The New York Times that Iranian hackers were likely behind the cyberattack.

The newspaper reported that three state officials briefed on an investigation into the cyberattack said the tradecraft used and the absence of a ransom demand led analysts to initially determine Iran was involved. Officials also cautioned that the assessment could change as more data is collected by investigators, according to the newspaper.

"The FBI is aware of recent public reporting around Water and Wastewater sectors. The FBI and our interagency partners are fully engaged to protect critical infrastructure and we remain well-equipped to protect against cyber threats of all varieties," the FBI said in a statement to Fox News Digital on Friday.

IRAN-LINKED HACKERS TARGET US MEDICAL TECH COMPANY

The newspaper reported that the hackers targeted infrastructure used to manage and monitor water towers operated by municipal governments.

The mayor of the city of Braham, Nate George, said on Monday, a "plant operator found that the water tower was calling for water, but the well was not operating."

"After learning that similar problems were occurring in at least four other Minnesota communities, Braham staff determined that the plant’s computerized control system had been compromised," he continued.

"Public works isolated the affected system, restored a backup, and restarted the plant within approximately 90 minutes. While the plant was offline, residents continued receiving water from the city’s water tower. City administration temporarily requested that residents conserve water to prevent the tower’s limited supply from being exhausted," George added.

In a statement shared with Fox News Digital, MNIT noted that "the investigation remains active, and Minnesota has not attributed the activity to a specific actor."

MNIT said it "continues to collaborate with federal, state, local, Tribal, and private-sector partners to investigate the attack, support affected communities, and strengthen the security of Minnesota's critical infrastructure."

"Cyberattacks against critical infrastructure require a coordinated, whole-of-government response," John Israel, MNIT assistant commissioner and Minnesota chief information security officer, said in a statement. "MNIT is working side by side with our partners to share intelligence, support affected communities, and help utilities restore operations safely while strengthening defenses against future attacks."

LIVE UPDATES ON IRAN WAR: TRUMP ANNOUNCES HAMAS DISARMAMENT DEAL WHILE SAUDI ARABIA LAUNCHES RED SEA DEFENSE COALITION

Israel told the Times that the breach was first detected Sunday and that hackers targeted 36 municipal water systems.

"Minnesota was one of the early detectors of this, but we’re seeing that this same threat activity has likely been occurring in other states throughout the nation," he was quoted as saying.

Nick Andersen, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s (CISA) acting director, told the newspaper that the agency was aware of "multiple potential incidents affecting local water utilities."

In the days leading up to the incident, CISA issued an advisory warning U.S. organizations of "ongoing Iranian-affiliated cyber activity targeting internet-connected operational technology (OT) devices."

"Iranian cyber actors continue to target U.S. critical infrastructure, and the FBI is committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing costs on those responsible," Assistant Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI’s Cyber Division said in the advisory.

It stated that a "group of Iranian-affiliated actors" has "targeted devices spanning multiple U.S. critical infrastructure sectors, including Water and Wastewater Systems, Energy and Government Services and Facilities, to include local municipalities."

item.title: Ryan Gosling's family-first philosophy reshaped his Hollywood career: experts
item.description: From "Barbie" to "Ghost Rider," Ryan Gosling's pivot toward blockbuster franchises traces back to a deliberate family-first philosophy he embraced as a dad.
item.content:encoded:
Ryan Gosling is officially joining the Marvel Cinematic Universe as Ghost Rider, marking the latest chapter in a career evolution that the actor has linked directly to fatherhood.

Earlier this month, Gosling, 45, made a surprise appearance during Marvel Studios' panel at San Diego Comic-Con where it was announced that he will be starring as the titular motorcycle-riding supernatural hero in a standalone "Ghost Rider" movie slated for release in 2028.

Gosling's casting comes as the three-time Oscar nominee continues to embrace blockbuster franchises after spending years building his reputation in some of Hollywood's darkest, most critically acclaimed dramas.

MARVEL STAR VINCENT D’ONOFRIO SAYS HE ‘CAN’T DO’ KINGPIN TRANSFORMATION ANYMORE

The actor has previously shared that his pivot toward lighter, more mainstream projects was intentional, explaining that his priorities changed after becoming a parent. Gosling shares daughters Esmeralda, 11, and Amada, 10, with his longtime partner, Eva Mendes, 52.

During a 2024 interview with The Wall Street Journal, Gosling said he avoids psychologically heavy roles because he wants to be emotionally present for Mendes and their daughters.

"I don’t really take roles that are going to put me in some kind of dark place," Gosling said. "This moment is what I feel like trying to read the room at home and feel like what is going to be best for all of us. The decisions I make, I make them with Eva, and we make them with our family in mind first."

‘DUCK DYNASTY’ STAR SADIE ROBERTSON HUFF ADMITS ‘FEARS’ OVER PUTTING HER KIDS ON REALITY TV

While speaking with Fox News Digital, PR expert Sarah Schmidt shared her view that Gosling's family-first approach has reshaped not only the types of roles he is taking, but the purpose behind them.

"He began picking lighter roles to keep his mood stable for his family and also create art that they can be a part of," the president of Interdependence PR said.

Paul Dergarabedian, head of Marketplace Trends for Rentrak, said Gosling's evolving priorities reflect a broader pattern among actors whose careers change alongside their personal lives.

"It does feel as though he is gravitating toward movies that his kids could actually see and enjoy," Dergarabedian said. "That kind of evolution is not unique as we have seen it with other actors as they get older, start families, and begin making choices that reflect where they are in life, how they see the world, and how they want to be perceived both personally and professionally."

Gosling's shift toward family-friendly entertainment signals a full-circle career moment for the actor, who made his debut as a child performer on the Disney Channel's "The All-New Mickey Mouse Club." He later appeared in the children's TV shows "Are You Afraid of the Dark?" and "Goosebumps."

During a 2011 interview with The New York Times, Gosling recalled that he decided to pursue "serious acting" at age 19. After making his mainstream breakthrough in the hit 2004 romantic drama "The Notebook," the Canada native went on to establish himself as one of Hollywood's most respected dramatic actors with critically acclaimed films, including "Half Nelson," "Blue Valentine," "Drive," "The Place Beyond the Pines," "Blade Runner 2049" and "First Man."

In recent years, Gosling has charted a different course with starring roles in audience-friendly movies including "Barbie," "The Fall Guy," and "Project Hail Mary," and his upcoming turns in "Star Wars: Starfighter" and "Ghost Rider."

Ryan McCormick, co-founder of Goldman McCormick PR, said he believes Gosling has earned the creative freedom to balance blockbuster franchises with prestige films.

"Ryan has not only built a career of acclaimed roles, those films are often box office successes," McCormick told Fox News Digital. "He has attained a rare status where he can do a sandbox film like 'Ghost Rider' and also take a dramatic or independent role without any one performance limiting his future choices."

Dergarabedian noted that Gosling's career has long defied easy categorization, citing his performances in 2011's "Crazy, Stupid, Love" and 2016's "La La Land."

"Gosling has always been far more versatile than any single role would suggest," Dergarabedian said. "He has shown he can do comedy, as he did so memorably in ‘Crazy, Stupid, Love.'"

"Of course, he proved he could carry a musical with ‘La La Land,'" he added.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Dergarabedian pointed to Gosling's starring role in Nicolas Winding Refn's "Drive" as a pivotal moment that expanded audiences' perception of him beyond romantic leads and demonstrated his ability to tackle darker, action-oriented material.

"You really cannot put Gosling in a box. He has been able to move between genres and tones with a level of ease that very few actors can match," Dergarabedian said. "All that being said, you can definitely see a shift in tone at this stage of his career."

Gosling previously shared that "La La Land" was the first project he chose that reflected his changing priorities after becoming a father. While speaking with The Wall Street Journal, Gosling recalled thinking of how Esmeralda and Amada would enjoy watching him prepare for the role.

"It was just sort of like, ‘Oh, this will be fun for them, too, because even though they’re not coming to set, we’re practicing piano every day, or we’re dancing, or we’re singing,'" Gosling said.

The philosophy carried over to 2023's "Barbie," which Gosling said resonated with his daughters, who were already immersed in the world of Barbie dolls before he signed on to play Ken.

"Their interest in Barbie and their disinterest in Ken was an inspiration," Gosling said. "I thought they were already making little movies about their Barbies on the iPad when it happened, so the fact that I was going off to work to make one too, we just felt like we were aligned."

Though some fans initially criticized Gosling's casting as Ken, arguing he was too old to portray Barbie's iconic counterpart, the actor ultimately won over audiences with a performance that became one of the film's biggest highlights. "Barbie" went on to gross more than $1.4 billion worldwide and Gosling earned an Oscar nomination for best supporting actor, cementing the film as both a commercial and critical triumph.

Schmidt told Fox News Digital that she believes the film fundamentally changed the trajectory of Gosling's career.

"Gosling proved that just because he began his career as a critically acclaimed darling does not mean that he cannot also be an international franchise and blockbuster star," she said.

"'Barbie' paved the way," Schmidt continued. "Prior to that, Gosling was a serious actor who occasionally moonlighted in a rom-com. As it turns out, Ken can carry a billion-dollar movie. He was funny and self-aware, and it did not cost him any of his hard-earned credibility."

Gosling has continued to embrace projects that his daughters can share with him. While promoting "Project Hail Mary," he revealed that Esmeralda and Amada occasionally voiced his alien co-star Rocky during rehearsals and became some of the sci-fi adventure movie's earliest viewers.

"Sometimes when I was working, and I needed to sort of switch things up or whatever, my kids would come in, and I had an earpiece in my ear, and they would talk for Rocky, so I could talk to them as Rocky," Gosling told People in March.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"And there's some moments in the movie where I'm laughing or I'm just so charmed by him, which is like, it's actually my kids talking to me and helping me out," Gosling continued.

"They've seen many cuts of this film," he added of his daughters. "They've given me many notes."

Marvel's "Ghost Rider" marks the latest chapter in the blockbuster era that Gosling has spent years building. Gosling's role as Johnny Blaze/Ghost Rider in the superhero movie will also reunite him with director Shawn Levy after the two previously collaborated on "Star Wars: Starfighter," which hits theaters in May 2027.

"Wow, is this really happening?" Gosling told the crowd at Comic-Con after being unveiled as Ghost Rider by Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige.

"As you know, this is a character I’ve wanted to play for a very long time," he said.

Schmidt told Fox News Digital that she believes Gosling has found a way to balance artistic credibility with commercial success without losing sight of the priorities that reshaped his career.

"He became a dad first, actor second," Schmidt said. "He is building a filmography legacy that his kids can be part of and proud of."

Meanwhile, Dergarabedian said he believes Gosling's recent choices have also cemented his place among Hollywood's biggest stars.

"He has become a go-to actor for huge, audience-friendly studio films and major franchises because he occupies such a unique position within the public eye," Dergarabedian said. "He has credibility, he has charm, he has range, and he has that elusive movie-star quality that is increasingly rare today."

item.title: RFK Jr takes MAHA to the kitchen with HHS cooking series promoting healthy meals for under $5
item.description: Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and chef Andrew Gruel prepare crispy wild Alaskan salmon cakes in the premiere of HHS's new budget-friendly cooking series.
item.content:encoded:
Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is taking the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) agenda from policy into the kitchen with a new government-produced cooking series designed to show Americans how to prepare healthy meals for less than $5 a serving whenever possible.

The new series, "The Real Food Show," launched Thursday on the HHS website and YouTube.

The program is intended to inspire Americans to cook more meals at home using whole, minimally processed ingredients while proving that healthy eating can be practical, approachable and affordable for families, according to the agency.

SHARK WEEK FANS MAY WANT TO THINK TWICE BEFORE EATING THIS OCEAN PREDATOR, EXPERTS WARN

"Food should be the foundation of our health," Kennedy said in a statement announcing the series. 

"With 'The Real Food Show,' we're empowering Americans to take control of their health one meal at a time. Healthy eating doesn't have to be expensive, and cooking at home can be faster, easier and more rewarding than people think."

Each episode features Kennedy alongside "America's most celebrated chefs" preparing what HHS describes as wholesome, budget-friendly meals inspired by the principles of the MAHA movement.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

The agency said recipes are designed to cost less than $5 per serving whenever practical, with an emphasis on whole ingredients and home cooking.

Celebrity chef Andrew Gruel joins Kennedy in the premiere episode, where they prepare crispy wild Alaskan salmon cakes served with an apple, white bean and greens salad.

Gruel told Fox News Digital he joined the project because he believes its mission extends far beyond teaching recipes.

"I'm excited to be part of the premiere episode because I believe the message is much bigger than a cooking show," Gruel said.

CHEF SAYS 'HORRIBLE STOMACH PROBLEMS' LED HIM ON MAHA JOURNEY

Gruel said he hopes the series encourages more Americans to cook at home after years of relying on convenience foods and helps rebuild basic cooking skills that he believes have been lost.

"My hope is that this series helps demystify cooking and shows people that preparing crave-worthy, healthy meals doesn't require professional training or expensive ingredients," Gruel said.

The recipe is intended to demonstrate that nutritious meals can be both affordable and easy to make at home.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"We talk about seafood a lot because I'm a seafood junkie, and one of the things that actually drove me into the restaurant industry was understanding people need to eat more seafood, more of the right types of seafood," Gruel said in a segment from the debut episode.

Gruel selected salmon cakes because many home cooks find seafood intimidating despite how simple it can be to prepare, he told Fox News Digital.

"Salmon is also nutrient-dense, affordable (frozen is fine) and incredibly versatile," he said. "They're a great example of how you can take a high-quality protein, combine it with a handful of simple pantry ingredients and create a meal that's both satisfying and family-friendly."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The show's goal of keeping meals under $5 per serving may surprise some shoppers amid stubborn grocery prices, but Gruel said it's achievable.

"Yes, you can absolutely make this meal for under $5 per serving, particularly when using canned or frozen wild Alaskan salmon," he said.

"One of the biggest misconceptions is that eating healthy is always more expensive, but with a few basic cooking skills and a little planning, real food is often more affordable than people think."

Gruel said he hopes viewers walk away with what he calls "kitchen confidence."

"It's not about creating more Bobby Flays," he said. "It's about helping families realize they can cook nutritious, affordable meals at home using real ingredients."

item.title: Ben Sasse's latest pancreatic cancer update comes amid his stark warning about America's future
item.description: Ben Sasse says his tumors shrank by over 80% on a clinical trial drug as he battles metastatic pancreatic cancer and warns about China and AI.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: Battling Stage 4 pancreatic cancer, former Nebraska Sen. Ben Sasse is looking ahead with optimism for his own health but expressed less hope for America's future.

He cautioned that America's greatest challenges are still to come in a pre-recorded interview for the Western Conservative Summit in Lakewood, Colorado, exclusively shared with Fox News Digital.

"Pancreatic cancer is nasty, and I would never wish it on my worst enemy, but I also would never want to go back to a stage of my life where I didn't know the power of pancreatic cancer prayer," said Sasse, quoting Pastor Tim Keller at Redeemer Presbyterian Church in New York.

Sasse, 54, shared in December 2025 that he has metastatic pancreatic cancer, which has spread to multiple organs — including his liver and lungs. He was initially given three to four months to live but entered a clinical trial for a drug called daraxonrasib, an oral therapy (pill) that is designed to block the defective gene that triggers uncontrolled cellular growth.

PANCREATIC CANCER VACCINE SHOWS PROMISE IN FIRST HUMAN TRIAL, PREVENTING DISEASE IN HIGH-RISK PATIENTS

"My tumors have shrunk by over 80% in the six and a half months I've been on this drug," said Sasse in his update. "The drug has been amazing, and I'm grateful for that common grace extension of time." 

"We're a couple days away from being seven months since my diagnosis at three to four months to live."

Even as he reflected on his own mortality, Sasse said he's increasingly concerned about the country's future, cautioning that the U.S. must outcompete China, overhaul its failing schools and adapt to an AI-driven economy.

"I want the U.S. Via decentralized corporate structures to rule the world, not CCP, tyrannical, Maoist to rule of the world, and I think most middle powers, most countries in the world, know that somewhere between 25 years from now, we're going to say the world is Western/U.S. led," said Sasse.

CHINA IS BUILDING A MASSIVE SHIP THAT SHOULD SCARE AMERICANS ABOUT THE FUTURE

He describes a world that is led by the U.S. passing along values with free trade, the rule of law, transparency and acknowledgment of human rights.

The alternative would be "CCP led," said Sasse. "Which is them controlling all trade through Beijing."

From the campus of Colorado Christian University, where conservative leaders gathered for the Western Conservative Summit, Sasse also weighed in on the challenges facing higher education.

"Our educational systems are just a complete disaster," said Sasse.

The latest Nation's Report Card found that roughly one in three eighth graders cannot read at even a basic level, nearly 40% fall below basic in math, and fewer than one-third are proficient in reading, according to the National Assessment Governing Board report for 2025.

BEN SASSE CLAIMS PUBLIC SCHOOLS WERE CREATED TO SEPARATE CATHOLIC KIDS FROM PARENTS, PRIESTS

Sasse argued that academic benchmarks are too low and that increasing government spending on education has failed to improve student outcomes.

"The potential and the capacity of most souls and most brains is a lot more than that, and we've just got a disastrous system," said Sasse.

Sasse said that the rise of AI is going to "externalize a lot of IQ" changing what schools will teach.

He added that America is entering an AI revolution that will disrupt work, education, and global power.

"A hundred years from now, when we look back on our moment, we're not gonna talk about our politics very much. I think we're gonna talk about the fact that we are living through a technological revolution," said Sasse.

item.title: House Democrat blasted after early release law freed inmates later charged with murder
item.description: Rep. Nellie Pou's COVID-era prison release law freed more than 7,000 inmates early but multiple were later charged with murder, sparking GOP attacks.
item.content:encoded:
A COVID-era prison release law championed by Rep. Nellie Pou, D-N.J., is facing renewed scrutiny after multiple inmates freed early under the program were later charged with murder.

More than 7,000 inmates received an early release starting in November 2020 after then-Gov. Phil Murphy, D-N.J., signed legislation sponsored by Pou, then a New Jersey state senator.

Under the law, state inmates were eligible for early release via "public health emergency credits" if they had less than one year remaining on their sentences and had not been convicted of murder or sexual assault and were not sex offenders.

People serving time for other violent offenses — including aggravated manslaughter and kidnapping — could still receive a shortened sentence of up to eight months.

NORTH CAROLINA TEACHER'S KILLING REIGNITES SCRUTINY OF ROY COOPER'S CRIMINAL JUSTICE RECORD IN SENATE RACE

Two inmates released under the program later pleaded guilty to or were convicted in separate homicide cases. A third remains in custody awaiting trial on murder and conspiracy charges.

Supporters of the law, including the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), argued the measure was necessary to reduce the prison population amid concerns about overcrowding during the COVID-19 pandemic.

A smaller prison population, according to Pou, would "keep everyone, guards included, safer" from the virus, she wrote in a 2020 statement.

But the New Jersey Democrat has said little publicly about the law since multiple inmates released under the program were linked to grisly killings.

The legislation passed over objections from GOP lawmakers and some county prosecutors, who warned it could endanger public safety by releasing violent offenders early.

Jerry Crawford, 30, was arrested in the shooting death of an 18-year-old just two days after his release on parole supervision in November 2020.

Crawford, who had been serving a burglary sentence, would have otherwise remained incarcerated until the following month, according to the New Jersey Department of Corrections, NJ.com reported.

He is scheduled to stand trial in January 2027 on murder and conspiracy charges, according to New Jersey court records.

Another inmate, 31-year-old Ronny Paden, was released early in November 2020 after the COVID-era program shortened his sentence for aggravated assault and weapons offenses. Two months later, he shot and killed two men at a birthday party.

Paden later pleaded guilty to first-degree aggravated manslaughter and was sentenced to 12 years in state prison.

A third inmate, Theodore Luckey, 47, is serving life without parole after pleading guilty to two counts of first-degree murder.

NEWSOM-BACKED LAW LETS ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHILD RAPIST SEEK EARLY RELEASE AGAIN AS DA URGES 'STOP THE MADNESS'

Luckey attacked and killed an ex-boyfriend with a machete in August 2021, striking him more than 120 times, after being released from prison in May. Prosecutors also said he strangled another man in a hotel room shortly beforehand.

He was released from prison under the program eight months early after completing most of a 15-year prison sentence involving a burglary conviction and illegal possession of a deadly weapon, the New Jersey-based Asbury Park Press reported.

Republicans sharply criticized Pou’s embrace of the early prison release program that freed several repeat offenders.

"Instead of holding criminals accountable, soft-on-crime radical Nellie Pou spearheaded legislation that lets violent offenders off the hook and threatens the safety of law-abiding New Jerseyans," New Jersey Republican Chairwoman Christine Giordano Hanlon told Fox News Digital.

"Nellie is a threat to her constituents’ safety, and they’ll send her packing because of it," National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) spokeswoman Maureen O’Toole said.

A representative for Pou did not directly respond to a request for comment about whether the congresswoman believed the program proved successful, but emphasized Pou’s support for law enforcement and public safety.

"Just this year, Congresswoman Pou voted in favor of more than $253 million in funding to hire and rehire local police and to steer $13.5 million toward state law enforcement agencies to combat drug trafficking," Morghan Cyr, Pou’s campaign manager, said in a statement.

The GOP attacks come as Pou is seeking a second House term in a northern New Jersey House seat that President Donald Trump narrowly carried in 2024.

Pou, a member of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, has joined House Democratic leadership in voting against GOP-authored legislation ranging from cracking down on illegal immigration to targeting "soft-on-crime" policies in Washington, D.C.

Still, it remains unclear whether Pou will face a serious re-election threat.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report shifted the race in favor of Democrats earlier this year to "Likely Democrat," citing New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, D-N.J., carrying Pou’s district by nearly 20 points during the 2025 gubernatorial contest.

item.title: Michigan's new head coach pours cold water on Ohio State rivalry: 'Hate is a strong word'
item.description: Kyle Whittingham says he wants to beat Ohio State as badly as anyone in Ann Arbor but admits he hasn't learned to hate the Buckeyes just yet.
item.content:encoded:
Kyle Whittingham may not know it yet, but despite being on the sidelines for two Rose Bowls, he will be coaching the most important game of his life in November.

After 22 seasons with Utah, Whittingham made the move to Ann Arbor to take over the Michigan Wolverines following Sherrone Moore's firing.

It's a whole new world for Whittingham, with Michigan's rivalries perhaps stronger than any Utah has had.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

And of course, there's arguably the best rivalry in all of sports with Ohio State.

Whittingham, though, is not focused on the Buckeyes just yet.

"I haven't learned really much more than I already knew. It's a national game. Everybody knows about it. It's 'The Game' as we call it. It's of great importance to both sides, obviously. But I'm an old-school coach. We got 11 games that we play before that, so we're not going to get ahead of ourselves," Whittingham said at Big Ten Media Day this week.

"Make no mistake, I understand the implications that it has... Very well-versed in what it means, the intensity of it, the national allure that it has. Our players are the same. I mean, everybody knows that that game's looming out there. I think the best-case scenario comes down to that 12th game. That's for all the marbles in the Big Ten. I think that would be ideal. Hopefully that happens."

Later on, he was asked if he'd learned to "hate" Ohio State.

Not yet.

"Hate's a strong word," Whittingham admitted.

FORMER LSU STAR DEMETRIUS BYRD ARRESTED AFTER ALLEGEDLY PULLING KNIFE ON BUS: 'WHO WANTS TO DIE?'

"But I want to win that game as badly as anybody in Ann Arbor. And like I said early on, what better scenario would there be is if that game came down to the championship in the Big Ten? That would be outstanding. We'll see what happens."

The rivalry took its ugliest turn in recent memory during the 2024 edition, when the unranked Wolverines went to Columbus as three-touchdown underdogs and upset the second-ranked Buckeyes. An ugly brawl ensued after Michigan players planted the university's flag on the OSU logo at midfield that led to police using mace. Ohio State got the last laugh when it wound up winning the national title.

After Ohio State snapped its four–game losing streak this past November at The Big House, Michigan players guarded their own midfield logo.

So, given what's happened in the last couple of years, Whittingham will learn soon enough.

item.title: Woman's death at Boston home owned by Rep. Ayanna Pressley's husband ruled a homicide: officials
item.description: An 18-year-old woman found dead at a Mattapan home owned by Conan Harris, husband of Rep. Ayanna Pressley, has been ruled a homicide by authorities.
item.content:encoded:
The death of a woman found at a home owned by the husband of Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., has been ruled a homicide, authorities said.

Boston Police officers responded to a report of a shooting in the city's Mattapan neighborhood on July 18 at about 1:52 p.m. and found Yoseliani Ann Marte Ocasio, 18, with a gunshot wound. She was pronounced dead at the scene, officials said.

Her death was ruled a homicide on Thursday by the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, authorities said in a statement.

item.title: Trump unloads on Cornyn, ties AG nomination fight to bitter Texas primary
item.description: Trump accuses Sen. John Cornyn of blocking Todd Blanche's attorney general confirmation over the anti-weaponization fund and audit immunity disputes.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump unleashed more fury on a Senate Republican he worked to oust who is standing in the way of his personal lawyer becoming the next attorney general.

Trump unloaded on Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, over acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s stalled nomination Friday morning, a day after threatening to withdraw Blanche’s nomination from the Senate.

He accused Cornyn of previously having no issue with the nearly $2 billion anti-weaponization fund, one of the issues that he and Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., are trying to kill, before Trump endorsed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in their grueling primary showdown.

TRUMP THREATENS TO YANK HIS OWN AG NOMINEE AS GOP REVOLT GROWS

"John Cornyn never had a problem with the so-called ‘Fund,’ which will not benefit me, but rather the great American Patriots who were hunted down like dogs and whose lives were unfairly and illegally destroyed by the Crooked Joe Biden Administration, until after I decided to Endorse and Support his Republican Primary opponent in Texas, who easily won the Nomination for the United States Senate," Trump said on Truth Social.

Fox News Digital did not immediately receive comment from Cornyn’s office in response to Trump’s remarks.

Cornyn and Tillis are both pushing the Department of Justice (DOJ) and administration to provide explicit, written proposals to permanently nix and rewrite the anti-weaponization fund and Trump’s audit immunity, respectively, that were borne from his settlement deal with the IRS, which Blanche rolled out earlier this year.

DOJ BARS IRS FROM AUDITING TRUMP’S PRIOR TAX RETURNS IN SETTLEMENT ORDER SIGNED BY BLANCHE

The Texas Republican, in particular, wants changes to Trump’s audit immunity spelled out in the deal, and has so far not had his demands met as paper continues to flow back and forth between the lawmakers and administration.

But the lawmakers contend that there’s a force above Blanche that is thwarting the process and further slowing down his confirmation.

"I thought we were pretty close to landing the plane last night, but this morning there's been some more complications," Cornyn told reporters on Thursday. "I think if this were just between me and Todd Blanche, we would have worked this out. But apparently he's getting some pushback from higher-ups at the White House. I don't know who, but this doesn't need to be this hard."

WATCH: GOP HOLDOUT REJECTS TRUMP THREAT AS AG NOMINEE STANDOFF EXPLODES

Trump appeared unwilling to part with the fund, which has been condemned by Republicans and Democrats over concerns that it would dole out taxpayer dollars to rioters who stormed the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.

"I will always feel that these victims of government abuse should be paid back for what they were forced to endure, their lives have been ruined," Trump said. "Millions of people agree with me, as was proven in my landslide Presidential win, where this was a major subject of debate, and so did John Cornyn, until he lost his Election to an opponent that I Endorsed. Todd Blanche, a good man, should be immediately approved as U.S. Attorney General."

Both Cornyn and Tillis met with Blanche toward the end of the day Thursday to continue hashing out a path forward.

Meanwhile, Trump threatened to yank Blanche’s nomination from the Senate over the impasse after Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, postponed his confirmation hearing scheduled for Thursday.

His plan would be to wait until both Cornyn and Tillis are out of office next year. But, there’s no guarantee that the Senate would be more welcoming to Blanche after the midterm elections this November.

And Tillis and Cornyn aren’t the only Republicans with reservations about Blanche — Sens. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, and John Curtis, R-Utah, are both on the fence on whether to support him on a full floor vote in the Senate.

Given universal Democratic opposition, their resistance could sink his chances.

item.title: Colorado small town abandoned after all elected officials resign, water concerns grow
item.description: Hartman, Colorado, a town of 30 residents, was declared abandoned after all elected officials resigned and its water system became a health hazard.
item.content:encoded:
A small town in Colorado has been declared abandoned by the state after its remaining elected officials resigned, leading its troubled water system to become a "health hazard" to its residents, according to state officials.

The Office of the Colorado Secretary of State said the determination was made this week after a public hearing showed that "the Town of Hartman had no Board of Trustees or Town Clerk, was unable to hold a town election, and owned infrastructure critical for the treatment or delivery of water to residents."

"Importantly, not determining that the Town of Hartman is abandoned as contemplated by § 31-3-201(1)(b), C.R.S. (2026), would leave the residents in further legal limbo during a health hazard, with no authority to conduct business, hold elections, or fix their water infrastructure so that clean water can be delivered to the town residents," Deputy Secretary of State Andrew Kline wrote in an abandonment order. "Abandonment is the only legal mechanism in Colorado statute that creates an avenue for residents of the area to receive clean water."

DISNEYLAND GUESTS LEFT SCRAMBLING AFTER WATER OUTAGE SHUTS BATHROOMS AND RESTAURANTS

Hartman, which has a population of 30 in southeast Colorado, saw its three active trustees resign in January, a day after a brawl erupted between four women following a board of trustees meeting, according to The Denver Post.

"Our safety was more important than having a government," Pam Packer, one of the trustees who resigned, told the newspaper, which also reported that the mayor resigned in October and that Hartman previously was grappling with embezzlement allegations and restraining orders.

Kline said in the abandonment order that in mid-June, "Ms. Jessie Simmons, a self-attested resident, landowner, and elector of the Town of Hartman, submitted a written application to the Secretary of State for determination of abandonment for the Town of Hartman alleging that the town does not have a board of trustees or town clerk, is unable to hold an election, and owns and operates water infrastructure needed to treat and deliver water to residents."

"Ms. Simmons further asserted that as of time of her application, the Town of Hartman had lacked chlorine in its water for over one month and the water was not potable and 'smells horrible.’ She stated that the Town of Hartman had been under an order to boil water for months," he wrote.

EXPERTS REVEAL HOW TO AVOID DEADLY LEGIONNAIRES' DISEASE AS NYC OUTBREAK KILLS 5

At a hearing on July 13, Eric Bergman, the director of the Division of Local Government for the Department of Local Affairs, "testified that he has regional managers throughout the state, and one in Southeast Colorado that has worked extensively with the Town of Hartman for the last 5 or 6 years," according to Kline.

"Mr. Bergman also testified that since 2022, DOLA representatives have been in the Town of Hartman over 30 times helping with elections, turnover, recalls, resignations, budgets, audits, grant administration, and training of new officials. In January of 2026, DOLA received letters of resignation from each of the town's then-Trustees. Since the resignation of these elected officials, no government officials or government remain in the Town of Hartman," the order stated.

"There are no government officials in the Town of Hartman who are authorized to approve contracts, spend funds, appoint replacements, certify elections, or make decisions regarding the Town of Hartman's water system. Mr. Bergman testified there is also no clerk or governing body to call, conduct, or certify a municipal election," it continued.

"According to Mr. Bergman, the Town of Hartman is facing a public health threat. Mr. Bergman testified that the Town of Hartman has been on a boil advisory since last October 2025, and the water currently needs testing and chlorine. The water tank is compromised and needs repair or replacement," Kline also wrote in the order. "There is no one operating the water system at this time. DOLA, along with the Colorado Department of Health and Environment had previously provided grants for more than $1 million to the Town of Hartman to work on the water system. Those funds were reimbursement-based. However, without government officials, the Town is unable to enter any contracts that would enable it to access the grant funds."

The Office of Colorado’s Secretary of State said that, following the abandonment order, "All existing streets, avenues, and alleys previously located within the abandoned town that are not owned by a third party shall be vested in the Board of County Commissioners of Prowers County," and that "Ownership of water infrastructure critical for the treatment or delivery of water to residents shall be vested in Prowers County, which shall transfer said infrastructure to an entity whose primary purpose is water treatment or delivery."

item.title: Firebrand rep unloads on socialist prime minister as 'hordes of military aged men' swarm European country
item.description: Viral video shows tens of thousands of migrants storming Spain's Ceuta enclave from Morocco as Rep. Brandon Gill blames Pedro Sánchez's amnesty program.
item.content:encoded:
As shocking videos circulate of migrants pouring over the collapsed border of the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, took a swipe at the country’s socialist prime minister, saying, "That's what happens every single time a politician offers amnesty."

Ceuta, a Spanish territory on the tip of Africa, formally requested a national emergency declaration on Thursday after about 60,000 migrants crossed the border from Morocco in the past several weeks. Video shows hordes of men smiling and posing for cameras, some carrying swimming flippers, and sprinting through the streets as authorities struggle to corral the unruly masses. Other footage shows crowds of migrants emerging from the sea, climbing up onto Ceuta's rocky shores and working their way around border fences.

Gill, a young Republican known for his viral takedowns during congressional hearings, blamed the breakdown on Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who leads the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party.

"Spain's socialist Prime Minister announced he would be giving amnesty to millions of illegal aliens. Now, his country is being invaded by hordes of military aged men from Africa," Gill posted on X. "Because that's what happens every single time a politician offers amnesty."

WISCONSIN DEM SOCIALIST GUBERNATORIAL HOPEFUL DODGES WHETHER SHE STILL WANTS TO ‘ABOLISH POLICE’

Sánchez's socialist government launched an "extraordinary regularization" program earlier this year that allows eligible undocumented migrants already living in Spain to obtain legal residence and work authorization. The government says the policy promotes economic integration, while critics describe it as a mass amnesty.

Ceuta President Juan Jesús Vivas formally requested that Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez declare a national emergency to help respond to the border crisis, Spanish media outlets reported. Madrid, however, denied the request.

"The declaration of a national emergency is part of the state civil protection regulations, which do not consider migratory flows as a risk to the National Civil Protection System, nor do they establish special plans, basic guidelines, or specific civil protection instruments for their management. Therefore, it is not possible to activate this mechanism, as requested by the president of the Government of Ceuta, Juan Jesús Vivas," Spain's Ministry of the Interior said in a statement, according to Spanish outlet El Pais.

Ceuta’s government, in their request for a national emergency declaration, noted that immigration from Morocco is always a problem for the Spanish enclave, but claimed the last 10 days represented a peak "of particular intensity." That peak has seen about 60,000 migrants cross the border in the past 10 days. 

EU ADMITS IT ‘DIDN’T HAVE CONTROL’ ON MIGRATION AS BLOC RUSHES CRACKDOWN AHEAD OF NEW RULES

"The Government of Spain is fully committed to providing an immediate response to the situation in Ceuta. We are mobilizing all necessary resources, working with Moroccan and international authorities, and preparing the necessary measures to restore normalcy as soon as possible," Sánchez wrote in a Thursday post on X.

Back in the U.S., the White House has also criticized Sánchez for the collapse, saying in a statement that "President Trump has long warned Europe what would happen if they continue to implement far-left, globalist policies – including enabling mass migration."

"Spain and other countries who have adopted this destructive philosophy should immediately reverse course or risk their own demise," said the White House.

TRUMP CRITICIZES SPAIN AMID IRAN, NATO RIFT AS PM SANCHEZ FACES QUESTIONS OVER POLITICAL MOTIVES

Sánchez, however, has previously claimed that accepting migrants is necessary to keep Spain's economy alive, arguing the country's low birth rates necessitate accepting immigrants.

"The West needs people. Currently, few of its countries have a rising population growth rate. Unless they embrace migration, they will experience a sharp demographic decline that will prevent them from keeping their economies and public services afloat. Their gross domestic product will stagnate. Their public healthcare and pension systems will suffer. Neither AI nor robots will be able to prevent this outcome... The only option to avoid decline is to integrate migrants in the most orderly and effective way possible," Sánchez wrote in a February op-ed in The New York Times.

Fox News Digital's Robert McGreevy contributed to this report.

item.title: Jemele Hill takes aim at Sophie Cunningham as Storm controversy grows over girls supporting women’s sports
item.description: Jemele Hill accused Sophie Cunningham of "ducking the smoke" after the Indiana Fever shielded her from postgame questions about a rally in Seattle.
item.content:encoded:
Disgraced former ESPN commentator Jemele Hill's response to the Sophie Cunningham controversy says more about today's sports media than it does about the Indiana Fever guard.

Cunningham is under fire for defending women's sports and Hill wasted little time weighing in.

Following Indiana's 105-95 win over Seattle, a reporter questioned Fever head coach Stephanie White about a "Support Sophie Cunningham" rally outside Climate Pledge Arena.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM RALLY ROCKS WNBA GAME AS 'SAVE WOMEN'S SPORTS' ACTIVISTS FACE COUNTERPROTEST

A spokesperson stepped in to answer with a prepared statement from the Fever.

"Neither our organization nor Sophie had any knowledge of this demonstration and no contact with its organizers. Our only goal as a team, whether at home or away, is to win basketball games and make Fever fans for life, and we are united in that mission."

Posting on X, Hill accused Cunningham of "ducking the smoke" while claiming the Fever betrayed Stephanie White and the rest of the team by shielding Cunningham from questions.

JEMELE HILL IS RIGHT: WNBA FANS EXPECT JOURNALISTS TO BE 'CHEERLEADERS,' AND THAT'S NOT HOW THIS WORKS

"Just a couple weeks ago, Sophie Cunningham was asked about the negative attention the W receives and she essentially said, that's part of the job and she realizes she's an entertainer. Cool.

"She's building an entire brand on being outspoken and yet when the smoke came, she ducked it. The Fever betrayed their other players and Stephanie White by putting them in a position to answer to something they didn't say."

Hill went a step further, arguing a WNBA reporter was justified in pressing the Fever about the rally during the postgame media session.

STORM CO-OWNER SUSPENDED AFTER INCIDENT WITH SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM FANS AS STAR BREAKS SILENCE ON CONTROVERSY

"Roberta [reporter] had every right to ask these questions. The Sophie Cunningham rally happened at this game. If a rally is taking place outside the arena, you don't wait until later to ask about it.

"If Sophie Cunningham is going to build a brand behind being outspoken, her and the Fever are going to have to take the shit that comes with it. Don't be in it for the jersey sales and then when people start asking questions, you want to run. It doesn't work that way."

Hill's posts also drew criticism from some users on X.

One reply read: "Another pretty white girl you got beef with. Color me surprised."

Another responded, "[Sophie] already said 'I said what I said' a 2nd time. Why do we need to hear it a third time?"

The controversy began days earlier, when Cunningham told ESPN she opposes trans athletes who are biologically male competing against women in women's sports.

Those comments sparked a grassroots movement in support of Cunningham, culminating in a "Support Sophie Cunningham" rally outside Climate Pledge Arena before the Fever's road matchup against the Storm. The support extended inside the arena, where two teenage girls held up a sign reading: "THANK YOU SOPHIE FOR SPEAKING UP FOR GIRLS."

The movement isn't slowing down. Additional "Support Sophie Cunningham" rallies are already planned ahead of upcoming Fever games in Oregon and Minnesota.

Instead of simply letting the girls enjoy the game, Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton confronted them and unleashed a string of expletives. According to one of the girls, the confrontation left her in tears.

One of the girls later recalled, "Yeah, I've never been yelled at like that... I thought she was going to be nice and then she starts screaming at us and cussing at us."

Brandi Kruse, who witnessed the exchange, pushed back as it unfolded. "Some of the fans were relentlessly booing at them," Kruse said. "And I kind of turned around and said, 'Look, they're just teenage girls.'"

The WNBA later fined the Storm $25,000 and suspended Keaton for five games over the incident.

The Fever maintained that neither the organization nor Cunningham had any knowledge of or contact with the rally's organizers.

Cunningham later addressed the controversy on social media, where she condemned Keaton's behavior.

She wrote on X: "I truly believe there is a safe space and love for EVERYBODY. Biological girls, biological boys, trans women, and trans men. Everyone is welcome at my table! You can disagree and still be kind.

"Bravo to those girls for standing up for what they believe. You'll be hearing from me soon. Yay for gifts. Truly embarrassing of the co-owner. Unfortunately shows the type of leader she is."

When WNBA players engage in left-wing activism, sports outlets praise their "authenticity" and defend their right to privacy when controversy hits.

Cunningham, however, received no such grace after speaking out in defense of women's sports.

Send us your thoughts: alejandro.avila@outkick.com / Follow along on X: @alejandroaveela

item.title: Texas teen bitten by barracuda in popular vacation spot after bracelet glints in water
item.description: A shiny bracelet likely attracted the barracuda that bit a 13-year-old girl's hand in Turks and Caicos. After surgery on her hand, the girl's mom spoke with Fox News Digital.
item.content:encoded:
A Texas teenager is recovering after being bitten by a barracuda while vacationing in Turks and Caicos.

Sugar Land resident Claire Macdonel, 13, was swimming in shallow water when the fish bit her hand on Sunday, July 19.

The teen was wearing a shiny bracelet on one of her wrists — which likely reflected light and was mistaken by the barracuda for prey. 

SHARK WEEK DANGERS HIT HOME AS MAN IS BADLY BITTEN WHILE SAVING PREGNANT FIANCÉE FROM HARM

Jen Macdonel, Claire Macdonel's mother, told Fox News Digital that the barracuda attack lacerated four of her daughter's tendons, in addition to a nerve and a ligament. The girl had surgery on Wednesday. 

"She could have easily lost her whole hand or fingers or worse," said Jen Macdonel. 

The teenager was doing handstands when a barracuda was likely attracted to the reflective items she was wearing, mistaking them for prey.

"You know, you're doing handstands against white sand, clear water, the sun hits that — she probably just looked like a disco ball," Jen Macdonel said.

RECORD SEAWEED INVASION LEAVES BEACHGOERS GAGGING AS FUMES RAISE HEALTH FEARS

Photos shared by the family show Claire Macdonel's hand covered in cuts and puncture wounds shortly after the bite. She wore a cast afterward as her wounds healed.

Claire Macdonel told Fox News Digital, "I just felt a lot of pressure. And then I went up. I saw my hand bleeding a lot, and I said, 'Mom, something bit me. I don't know what to do.'"

(WARNING, GRAPHIC IMAGE BELOW:)

"I looked behind me and saw a big silver tail. ... I was very scared," she told FOX 26 Houston.

"I was just anxious, like, I was crying the whole time," she said. 

SHARK WEEK SHOCKER AS GREAT WHITE BREACHES JUST YARDS FROM OBLIVIOUS BOOGIE BOARDER

A nurse who had been in the water nearby — an "angel," as the teen described her — saw the commotion and rushed over. The woman applied a tourniquet to Claire Macdonel's injured hand while the girl's mother worked hard to understand what had just happened. 

BOY STUMBLES ON STRANGE BEACH OBJECT IDENTIFIED AS RARE 1.8M-YEAR-OLD FOSSIL

The nurse "really saved the day," Jen Macdonel told Fox News Digital.

"I was in shock, actually … I just kind of had an out-of-body experience where I knew I had to stay calm. Your mom instincts kick in," she said. 

"I was very afraid of how much blood she was losing during all of that time. I didn't know if she was going to lose her hand or her fingers or worse," the mother said.

She said she was trying not to panic, but it was a struggle.

"I was constantly looking for signs of infection," Jen Macdonel said.

She told Fox News Digital her daughter hopes to spread awareness about what could happen to others in the water, also emphasizing that the barracuda attack hasn't diminished her daughter's love of the water.

"She's already planning our next trip so we can have a redo because we love the island, and she loves the water," Jen Macdonel said. 

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Ever since I got this bite, it has actually made me want to discover the ocean even more ... I'm even more curious about what's inside the ocean and what behavior it has," Claire Macdonel told Fox News Digital.

"I've always loved marine life, even if it's scary fish. I've always been curious about them."

Her mom added, "Something terrifying happened. It was unfortunate, but it is rare, and we don't want to create fear for the ocean because she got right back in the ocean."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Barracudas "stay still and wait for prey to swim past," said Yannis Papastamatiou, an associate professor in biological sciences at Florida International University.

Papastamatiou told Fox News Digital that barracudas respond "immediately" to anything they perceive as prey, though attacks on humans are very rare.

"For the most part, we are clearly much too large to be considered prey," he said. "But if you are wearing anything shiny, they may perceive that as the movement of a smaller fish and respond."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"The main thing is I would avoid wearing anything reflective like jewelry," Papastamatiou added. 

"If you do see a barracuda, then just avoid making sudden movements. Remember their vision is not good like ours, and they may think your hand is small prey. Barracuda bites are actually very rare."

The incident came just weeks after Turks and Caicos made international headlines for a different reason.

Earlier this summer, the U.S. State Department renewed its Level 2 "Exercise Increased Caution" travel advisory for the Caribbean destination, citing reports of assaults, petty crime and scams targeting tourists.

item.title: The real reason Americans are fleeing blue states for Florida and Texas

This month, New York Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli launched a taxpayer migration dashboard showing the number of people leaving his state. To the surprise of few, New York is hemorrhaging residents, especially from its middle class. DiNapoli put it plainly: "I remain very concerned about the net loss of married, middle-class filers, and urge policymakers to continue their efforts to improve affordability for New York's families."

My own analysis of five years of nationwide IRS records — covering every move made by every American taxpayer between 2018 and 2023 — confirms what these families already know. Nurses in Queens and firefighters in Los Angeles understand better than anyone that working-class paychecks don't buy middle-class lives anymore.

Yet the statistics also offer new insights into what’s happening.

NEW YORK CITY LOST RESIDENTS ACROSS ALL INCOME LEVELS LAST YEAR, STUDY FINDS

Over those five years, California lost more than 1.2 million people. On balance, almost 1.7 million residents of New York, Massachusetts and Illinois also took their tax dollars, spending and income elsewhere. Florida gained more people than any other state, while Idaho, South Carolina, Delaware and Montana were other popular destinations.

When I went looking for the precise reasons people moved, the usual suspects didn't quite hold up. It wasn't the weather. It wasn’t partisan lean. It wasn't even the cost of living, strictly speaking.

States with lower taxes gained residents. So did states with freer labor markets and abundant housing. Those with high taxes, government barriers to finding careers and excessive constraints on building homes lost people. The pattern held even after accounting for the other explanations people often reach for first.

BLUE-STATE TAX BURDEN FUELS AMERICANS FLEEING TO REPUBLICAN-LED SOUTHERN STATES

This points to a lesson that blue-state lawmakers who try to manufacture affordability through government spending and mandates never seem to understand. People go where it's simpler and easier to earn a living, buy a home and build a career. It’s that easy.

Every few hundred dollars the taxman doesn’t take can mean a week’s groceries, a car payment or back-to-school clothes. States that respect the sweat equity of their workers are winning the migration race. Florida, Texas, Tennessee and half a dozen others have no state income tax. A married couple earning $100,000 in New York City owes $6,668 more in income taxes every year than it would owe in one of the nine states without an income tax. At $150,000, that difference jumps to $11,338.

However, it isn’t just taxes that determine where people move. Affordable housing gets them to settle. My research shows that states issuing more building permits — those where it's actually possible to build new homes without a multiyear fight at the local zoning board — gained more residents than states measured by any other factor.

THE KEY STRATEGY RED STATES ARE USING TO LOWER HOUSING COSTS REVEALED

When a state makes it hard to build — or allows its municipal authorities to run amok — home prices climb, and workers move to states where builders can keep up with demand. Idaho, South Carolina and Florida make it relatively easy to build. Once again, New York and California make it difficult, and their mistake shows up every year in the form of moving trucks heading for the state line.

Freedom to work matters, too. States that make it easier to hire, get licensed and start a business also saw strong gains, even after accounting for everything else.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

For example, Virginia requires licenses for 72 different occupations. Workers in these fields face an average of 580 days of education and experience requirements, compared with only 228 days in North Carolina. Why would a worker — one who may already be qualified — choose to move somewhere that requires an extra year of training?

Running through all of this is the same lesson: The more freely a state’s residents can work, build and earn, the more likely the state is to retain the families who power its economy in the first place. Most Americans aren't leaving high-tax, housing-constrained states because of the weather, and they're not moving to Florida or Texas by accident. They're following paychecks and mortgages they can actually afford.

Thomas DiNapoli is right to be worried about New York's future, and the fix isn't complicated. Cut the tax burden, let builders build and get out of the way of work. Or watch the moving trucks pull away.

item.title: Red Sox fans beg team to trade 'toxic' Jarren Duran after yet another embarrassing incident
item.description: Jarren Duran's dugout blowup over Willson Contreras not scoring adds to a long list of incidents as the MLB trade deadline approaches for Boston.
item.content:encoded:
No team in baseball is more sad to see July end than the Boston Red Sox.

With one day left in the month, the Sox have surged in the American League, going a stunning 25-5 since June 25, including a 15-game win streak that was snapped last week.

In the last six weeks, Boston has gone from arguably the worst team in baseball, to a full two games up in the AL Wild Card race, and only seven games back in the division.

The team has gone from sellers to, reportedly, big-time buyers ahead of next week's trade deadline, as a three-game set with the LA Dodgers looms this weekend.

So, yeah — it's all ham & eggs right now in Boston ...

... Except for one nagging thorn in the team's side.

Yes, once again, outfielder Jarren Duran is becoming a headache:

Lordy. I watched that play live, and I was stunned. I couldn't believe Jarren Duran was actually upset that Willson Contreras didn't score from third on what was essentially a pop-up to left field.

I thought I was seeing things. I thought I was going crazy.

But no, he was legit angry at either A) Contreras for not trying, or B) third base coach Chad Epperson for not sending a 34-year-old first baseman on a ball that was caught 20-feet behind him.

Either way, it was such a bad look for a player who has been a major headache for the Red Sox for the better part of three years now.

A constant, major headache.

There was the "incident" during an at-bat at Fenway Park a few years back where Duran was caught on a hot mic calling a fan a nasty name.

There was the incident in Cleveland last year with a fan. There was the other incident earlier this year in Minnesota, also with a fan. There was a THIRD incident, just last month, with a Yankees fan.

And now this.

Here's the thing ... the MLB trade deadline is next week. The Red Sox have a logjam of outfielders — all of them very good.

Except Duran, who is hitting an abysmal .195 in 101 games this season. Read that again.

.195!

For those wondering, that is the WORST average for a qualified hitter (3.1 plate appearances per game) in all of baseball.

The Red Sox traded Rafael Devers last summer because he was considered a problem in the clubhouse. At the time, Devers — the team's FRANCHISE player — was hitting around .280 with 15 home runs. And they traded him because he was a cancer in the clubhouse.

It's past time to deal with Duran. The production doesn't warrant the headache that comes with it. Anyone with eyeballs can see it.
